messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Malik, a 22-year-old school principal in a small district office on the edge of a busy African immigrant neighborhood, came to treatment after months of feeling as though the past was pressing into the present from every direction. He had grown up with a caregiver who beat him as a child, often in abrupt bursts that left no warning and no explanation, and he now described his world as being organized around the fear of the next unpredictable blow. What made the memories especially potent was not just the abuse itself but how they returned: old photos could stop him cold, and waking from a nightmare would leave him disoriented and on edge, as if he had been yanked back into an old room he could not quite see. In those moments, the event did not come back to him as a smooth story; it arrived in disconnected pieces that did not fit together, and because he could not deliberately pull the memory into a clear sequence when he tried, he was left with fragments that felt more real and vivid than ordinary memories, sharp enough to make him distrust what he was seeing around him.

The more Malik found himself caught by those fragments, the more he came to believe that something had been permanently altered in him. He would sit at his desk in the school office, looking over disciplinary reports or fielding sudden interruptions from staff, and the smallest unpredictability in the day could pull him into the same conclusion: he could not stop bad things from happening to him. A student arriving in tears without warning, a parent demanding to speak immediately, even a change in the schedule he had not anticipated could make his chest tighten with the old sense of helplessness. Because the memories came back in broken pieces, he struggled to place them safely in the past, and that uncertainty fed his fear that he had changed for the worse. He had come to believe that if he were pushed enough, his own anger might become dangerous; he worried that he would not be able to control it and would do something terrible. That fear did not stay abstract. When the memories felt especially vivid, he became more watchful for anything that might set him off, and he found himself bracing against ordinary moments, scanning faces and voices for signs that another blow, humiliation, or loss of control might be coming.

As the months went by, those fears shaped what Malik allowed himself to encounter. Old photographs were no longer casual reminders of family or childhood; he avoided looking through albums, and he would ask his partner to put away pictures from family gatherings if they surfaced on a phone screen. When his own mind felt unstable, he interpreted the old photos as evidence that the injured child was still present inside him, unchanged in the worst way, and that made the memories feel even more vivid and threatening. The nightmares had the same effect. He dreaded waking suddenly in the night because the residue of the dream made him feel as if something bad was about to happen, and by morning he was already prepared for danger. In the school building, unpredictable situations became increasingly hard to tolerate, so he began stepping back from hallway conflicts and delegating more than he used to, not because he lacked competence but because he feared what his body and mind might do under pressure. Yet every attempt to steady himself seemed to circle back into the same experience: the more he tried to keep the memory in order, the more it broke apart; the more it broke apart, the more convinced he became that he was damaged and at risk; and the more convinced he became, the more tightly he avoided the things that might remind him of it.

By the time he sought help, Malik was exhausted by how much space the fear had taken up in his work and his relationship. He cared deeply about his partner and wanted to stay present, but he was frightened that his irritability and constant anticipation of danger would spill into the people he loved or into the school community that relied on him. What finally brought him in was a night of waking from a nightmare and finding himself unable to settle, then spending the next day moving through the office with the old familiar sense that he could not stop bad things from happening. He hopes to understand why the memories remain so raw and why old photos, unexpected disruptions, and the shock of waking from dreams can still make him feel as though he is back in the hands of that childhood violence, and he is most afraid that the version of himself shaped by it will stay permanently in control.
